question: Slovo papuče k nám prišlo cez turečtinu až z perzštiny. Čo v perzštine doslova znamenalo?
source_excerpt: Greek papoutsi 'shoe' is borrowed from Turkish papuç 'slipper', from Persian pâpuš (literally 'foot-cover').

extra.why_interesting: Players treat 'papuče' as a cosy, homely, thoroughly Slovak word. It is actually a Persian compound that arrived through Turkish. Its literal meaning is simple enough to guess once you are told it is foreign, and the pyjama link adds a second surprise.
extra.verification_notes: Persian pāpūš is literally 'foot-cover' (pā 'foot' + pūš 'covering'), and Turkish papuç derives from it, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eggplant_papoutsaki; I found no Slovak-specific source.

explanation: Perzské pápúš sa skladá z pá, teda noha, a púš, teda zakryť. To isté perzské slovo pre nohu sa skrýva aj v pyžame, ktoré doslova znamená odev na nohy.

question: V Japonsku sa doma vyzujete a obujete si papuče, ako sme zvyknutí aj u nás. Do jednej miestnosti však na vás čaká ešte samostatný pár papúč, ktorý z nej nesmiete vyniesť. Ktorá miestnosť to je?
source_excerpt: Toilet slippers are a separate pair that stays in the restroom; the word 'toilet' is printed on them.

extra.why_interesting: Slovaks already know the custom of changing into slippers at home and assume one pair is enough. The idea of a second pair that never leaves one room is a delightful extra step. The player can work out which room it is from hygiene logic.
extra.verification_notes: Separate toilet slippers that must stay in the toilet room are standard Japanese etiquette, per https://thedragontrip.com/blog/japan/the-backpackers-guide-to-etiquette-in-japan/.

explanation: Pri dverách záchoda stoja špeciálne záchodové papuče, aby sa nečistota nerozniesla po byte. Kto v nich omylom vyjde do obývačky, spraví klasický trapas cudzinca.
